Polynomial Stein operators: a noncommutative algebra perspective

Ehsan Azmoodeh ††thanks: Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 7ZL, United Kingdom. E-mail: ehsan.azmoodeh@liverpool.ac.uk    Dario Gasbarra ††thanks: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Helsinki, B314, FI-00014 Helsinki, Finland. E-mail: dario.gasbarra@helsinki.fi    Robert E. Gaunt ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, The University of Manchester, M13 9PL Manchester, United Kingdom. E-mail: robert.gaunt@manchester.ac.uk
Abstract

In this paper, we make a novel connection between Stein’s method and noncommutative algebra by viewing polynomial Stein operators (Stein operators with polynomial coefficients) as elements of the first Weyl algebra. Through this connection we study the algebraic structure of classes of polynomial Stein operators. In the case of the standard Gaussian distribution, we provide a complete description of the corresponding class of polynomial Stein operators by (i) identifying it as a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R} with an explicit given basis and (ii) by showing that this class is a principal right ideal of the first Weyl algebra generated by the classical Gaussian Stein operator ∂−x\partial-x, with ∂\partial denoting the usual differential operator. We also study the characterising property of polynomial Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution, and give examples of general classes of polynomial Stein operators that are characterising, as well as classes that are not characterising unless additional distributional assumptions are made. By appealing to a standard property of Weyl algebras, we shown that the non-characterising property possessed by a wide class of polynomial Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution is a consequence of a general result that is perhaps surprising from a probabilistic perspective: the intersection between the class of polynomial Stein operators for any two target distributions with holonomic densities or holonomic characteristic functions is non-trivial.

Keywords: Stein’s method; non-commutative algebra; Weyl algebra; Gaussian integration by parts; holonomic function
MSC 2010: Primary 16S32; 60E05; Secondary 60F05

1 Introduction

We begin with the following definitions that play a pivotal role in this paper. The first definition concerning polynomial Stein operators is taken from our recent paper [AGG23a]. All random variables throughout the paper are real-valued.

Definition 1.1.

Let XX be a (continuous) target random variable. Let T≥1T\geq 1. We say that a linear differential operator S:=SX=∑t=0Tpt∂tS:=S_{X}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t} acting on a suitable class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions is a polynomial Stein operator for XX if :

  • (a)

    S​f∈L1​(X)Sf\in L^{1}(X),

  • (b)

    I​E​[S​f​(X)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[Sf(X)\right]=0 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, and

  • (c)

    the coefficients ptp_{t}, t=0,1,…,Tt=0,1,\ldots,T, are polynomial.

By PSOℱ​(X)\mathrm{PSO}_{\mathcal{F}}(X) we denote the set of all polynomial Stein operators, acting on a class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions, for the target random variable XX. Hereafter, for the ease of notation, we write PSOℱ​(X)=PSO​(X)\mathrm{PSO}_{\mathcal{F}}(X)=\mathrm{PSO}(X).

Definition 1.2 (Characterising polynomial Stein operators).

We say that an operator S∈PSO⁡(Y)S\in\mathrm{PSO}(Y) is a characterising Stein operator for the target random variable YY if, for any given random variable XX such that S​f∈L1​(I​PX)Sf\in L^{1}({\rm I\kern-1.60004ptP}_{X}) for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, the condition

I​E​[S​f​(X)]=0,∀f∈ℱ{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[Sf(X)\right]=0,\quad\forall\,f\in\mathcal{F}

implies X=dYX=_{d}Y (equality in distribution).

Remark 1.1.

Observe that 0∈PSO⁡(X)0\in\mathrm{PSO}(X) is a trivial (and non-characterising) Stein operator for the target random variable XX.

Remark 1.2 (Note on the class of functions ℱ\mathcal{F} I).

Consider the Stein operator S=∑t=0Tpt∂tS=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t} for the random variable XX supported on I⊆ℝI\subseteq\mathbb{R}. In the Stein’s method literature, a commonly used choice of test functions is the class ℱS,Y\mathcal{F}_{S,Y} which contains all functions f∈CT​(I)f\in C^{T}(I) such that 𝔼​|Xj​f(t)​(X)|<∞\mathbb{E}|X^{j}f^{(t)}(X)|<\infty, j=0,…,mj=0,\ldots,m, T=0,…,TT=0,\ldots,T, where m=max0≤t≤T​deg​(pt)m=\mathrm{max}_{0\leq t\leq T}\,\mathrm{deg}(p_{t}). Examples of other suitable classes of functions and clarifications on the classes of functions used in this paper are given in Remark 1.3 at the end of the Introduction.

Polynomial Stein operators lie at the heart of Stein’s method [Ste72] and the Nourdin-Peccati Malliavin-Stein method [NP09, NP12], powerful techniques for proving quantitative probabilistic limit theorems. Indeed, the starting point of Stein’s method for Gaussian approximation [Ste72, CGS11, NP12] is the following characterisation of the standard Gaussian distribution, known as Stein’s Lemma. Consider the divergence operator G=∂−xG=\partial-x, where ∂=dd​x\partial=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} denotes the usual differential operator. Then, a real-valued random variable XX is equal in distribution to N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1) if and only if I​E​[G​f​(X)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Gf(X)]=0 for all absolutely continuous f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that I​E​|f′​(N)|<∞{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}|f^{\prime}(N)|<\infty.

Motivated by Stein’s Lemma, [Ste72] introduced the so-called Stein equation G​f​(x)=h⁡(x)−𝔼⁡[h⁡(N)]Gf(x)=h(x)-\mathbb{E}[h(N)], where h:ℝ→ℝh:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a test function. Evaluating both sides of the Stein equation at a random variable of interest WW and taking expectations now yields the transfer principle

𝔼⁡[h⁡(W)]−𝔼⁡[h⁡(N)]=𝔼⁡[G​fh​(W)],\mathbb{E}[h(W)]-\mathbb{E}[h(N)]=\mathbb{E}[Gf_{h}(W)], (1.1)

where fh(x)=−ex2/2∫−∞x{h(t)−𝔼[h(N)]}e−t2/2dtf_{h}(x)=-e^{x^{2}/2}\int_{-\infty}^{x}\{h(t)-\mathbb{E}[h(N)]\}e^{-t^{2}/2}\,dt solves the Stein equation G​f​(x)=h⁡(x)−𝔼⁡[h⁡(N)]Gf(x)=h(x)-\mathbb{E}[h(N)]. Many important probability metrics, including the Kolmogorov, total variation and Wasserstein distances, can be expressed as integral probability metrics of the form suph∈ℋ|𝔼⁡[h⁡(W)]−𝔼⁡[h⁡(N)]|\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathbb{E}[h(W)]-\mathbb{E}[h(N)]| where the supremum is taken over some class of functions ℋ\mathcal{H}, e.g., taking ℋK={𝟏⋅≤z|z∈ℝ}\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{K}}=\{\mathbf{1}_{\cdot\leq z}\,|\,z\in\mathbb{R}\} induces the Kolmogorov distance. Thus the problem of bounding the distance between the distributions of WW and NN with respect to an integral probability metric reduces to bounding the quantity 𝔼⁡[G​fh​(W)]\mathbb{E}[Gf_{h}(W)] for a given h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and then taking the supremum over all h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}. This procedure has proven to be remarkably effective in the context of Gaussian approximation, partly on account of the fact that the quantity 𝔼⁡[G​fh​(W)]\mathbb{E}[Gf_{h}(W)] is expressed as an expectation of just the random variable WW; the Gaussianity of the limit random variable NN is encoded in the operator GG. More generally, this procedure can be applied for other limit distributions, in which a suitable Stein operator SS (that is preferably shown to be characterising) takes the place of Stein’s classical operator GG.

Stein operators have classically been used as part of Stein’s method to establish explicit bounds in distributional approximations, finding applications in fields as diverse as random graph theory [BHJ92], algebra [FR22] and number theory [Har09]. In recent years, there has also been a growing trend in which Stein operators have found applications beyond proving quantitative limit theorems, with examples including relaxing the Gaussian assumption in shrinkage [FGRS22], new tests for goodness-of-fit [Ana23] and new methods for parameter estimation [EFGPS].

Whilst researchers have been successfully applying Stein’s method for over 50 years, mysteries about the method itself abound. One such mystery (Q1) is: why does the Stein operator G=∂−xG=\partial-x work so well for normal approximation? This is true for most other distributions in that, in the current literature, only one or two Stein operators tend to be useful in the context of distributional approximation for a given target distribution, even though there are infinitely many Stein operators for a given distribution. Related to this question, the following question is natural: can a description be given for a typical element of the class of polynomial Stein operators for a given distribution (Q2)? Another mystery surrounds the characterising nature of Stein operators. It is well-known that the standard Gaussian Stein operator G=∂−xG=\partial-x is characterising in the sense of Definition 1.2. However, does this remain true for all operators in the class PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) (Q3)? More generally, one can ask about the characterising nature of Stein operators for general continuous probability distributions. Within the Stein’s method community, speculations include: ‘all polynomial Stein operators are characterising, but it can just be difficult to prove this for a given Stein operator’ and ‘Stein operators are characterising if and only if the distribution is determined by its moments.’ In Theorem 5.1, we in fact see that the characterising property enjoyed by many Stein operators in the literature cannot be taken for granted (even for distributions that are determine by their moments): all classes of polynomial Stein operators for distributions with a holonomic density or holonomic characteristic function contain non-trivial elements that are not characterising.

In this paper, we provide, at least partial, answers to questions (Q1), (Q2) and (Q3). We do so by making a novel connection between Stein’s method and noncommutative algebra. In particular, we view polynomial Stein operators as elements of the first Weyl algebra, the ring of linear differential operators with polynomial coefficients (in one variable). Weyl algebras enjoy a rich algebraic structure and their properties are well-understood; we refer the reader to [Bjö79, Cou95, GW04, MR87, Lam01, CF08] and references therein for introductions and comprehensive accounts of the theory. For example, it is well-known that Weyl algebras are simple integral domains, Noetherian (left/right) and Ore extensions. Two-sided ideals of Weyl algebras have plain structure; however, the structure of one-sided ideals is less obvious. Forasmuch as being Noetherian implies all one-sided ideals are finitely generated; however, more delicately, a famous theorem by Stafford [Sta78] says that every one-sided (left/right) ideal of Weyl algebras can be generated by two elements. With this powerful theory at hand, we are able to address questions (Q1), (Q2) and (Q3) and consequently gain entirely new perspectives on Stein’s method, some of which are perhaps surprising from a probabilistic viewpoint.

For (Q1), we identify PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) as a principle right ideal of the first Weyl algebra generated by Stein’s classical operator G=∂−xG=\partial-x (see Theorem 3.1). Various interpretations have been given as to why GG is a natural object in Gaussian analysis via Stein’s method, such as the the generator approach to Stein’s method of [Bar88, Bar90, Göt91] in which (∂−x)∂(\partial-x)\partial is recognised as the generator of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with standard Gaussian stationary distribution, and the canoncial Stein operator viewpoint of [LRS17]. Here, we provide another such interpretation, which we consider to be fundamental and rather mathematically satisfying. Moreover, due to the aforementioned Stafford’s Theorem of [Sta78], the fact that every one-sided (left/right) ideal of Weyl algebras can be generated by two elements implies that for a given target random variable XX, the class PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) can be generated by two Stein operators (see Proposition 3.1). This result explains why, for a given continuous distribution, one would expect that only one or two polynomial Stein operators would prove to be most useful in the context of distributional approximation, despite the fact that there are infinitely many Stein operators for a given distribution.

We consider it to be a fundamental question as to whether the ideal PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X), for a given continuous random variable XX, is principle. In Section 3.3, we consider this question for the random variables Hp​(N)H_{p}(N), p≥1p\geq 1, where HpH_{p} is the probabilist’s Hermite polynomial of degree pp. These random variables are of fundamental importance in Gaussian analysis and Malliavin calculus, and appear as target distributions in the asymptotic theory of U-statistics (see [KBY94, Section 4.4] and [Lee90, Chapter 3]); however, the Malliavin-Stein method has yet to be adapted to these distributions for p≥3p\geq 3. In Examples 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 , we prove that the ideal PSO​(H2​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{2}(N)) is principle, whilst the ideals PSO​(H3​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{3}(N)) PSO​(H4​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{4}(N)) are not principle; we conjecture that PSO​(Hp​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{p}(N)) is principle if and only if p=1,2p=1,2 (see Remark 3.4).

For (Q2), we provide a complete algebraic description of the class PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) (Theorem 3.1). This theorem includes the aforementioned result that PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) is a principle right ideal of the first Weyl algebra generated by the operator G=∂−xG=\partial-x. We also show that PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) is a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R} with the operators S(k,t)=Hk∂t−Hk+t∈PSO(N)S(k,t)=H_{k}\partial^{t}-H_{k+t}\in\text{PSO}(N), k≥0k\geq 0, t≥1t\geq 1, forming a basis. Note that S⁡(0,1)=GS(0,1)=G. Whilst methods exist for obtaining families of Stein operators for a given target distribution (see the flexible approach to Stein’s density method of [LRS17, MRRS23] and our algorithmic approach [AGG23a]), this is the first time in the literature that a complete description has been given for the class of polynomial Stein operators for a given target distribution. Interestingly, the fact that S​(k,t)∈PSO​(N)S(k,t)\in\text{PSO}(N), which yields a useful integration by parts formula, was exploited by [Bar86] in order to derive asymptotic expansions for smooth functions of sums of independent random variables. We also remark that the Stein operators Sm=S(m−1,1)=Hm−1∂−HmS_{m}=S(m-1,1)=H_{m-1}\partial-H_{m} and Lm=S(0,m)=∂m−HmL_{m}=S(0,m)=\partial^{m}-H_{m}, m≥1m\geq 1, were also introduced as natural generalisations of the operator GG in the delightful paper [GR05].

In Section 3.1, we complement the algebraic descriptions of PSO​(Hp​(N))\text{PSO}(H_{p}(N)) given in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 by making a connection between Stein’s method and holonomic function theory, which allows us to provide simple conditions under which PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) is non-trivial for a given target random variable XX. As an example, in Corollary 3.1, we show that PSO​(h​(N))≠{0}\text{PSO}(h(N))\not=\{0\} for any h∈ℝ⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{R}[x] (the ring of polynomials with real-valued coefficients).

The characterising problem (Q3) is the subject of Sections 4 and 5. In Proposition 4.3, we show that the polynomial Stein operators Sm=Hm−1∂−HmS_{m}=H_{m-1}\partial-H_{m}, m≥1m\geq 1, are characterising in the sense of Definition 1.2. This is a consequence of a more general result that all polynomial Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution that are first order linear differential operators are characterising (see again Proposition 4.3). We remark that the Stein operators (∂−x)∂n(\partial-x)\partial^{n}, n≥0n\geq 0, that is the Stein operators for the Gaussian distribution with coefficients with polynomial degree one, are seen to be characterising as a direct consequence of Proposition 2.1 of our recent paper [AGG23b]. We also show that the Stein operators S(k,t)=Hk∂t−Hk+t∈PSO(N)S(k,t)=H_{k}\partial^{t}-H_{k+t}\in\text{PSO}(N), k,t≥1k,t\geq 1, are characterising amongst the class of symmetric and infinitely divisible distributions (Corollary 4.1). We conjecture that the additional assumptions of symmetric and infinitely divisible distributions are artefacts of our proof, and that these assumptions can be disposed of. However, it turns out that there are non-trivial elements of PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) that are not characterising unless additional distributional assumptions are made; in part (d) of Example 4.1, we give a general recipe for constructing such non-characterising polynomial Stein operators for the Gaussian distribution. This non-characterising property of elements of the class PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) is in fact a special case of the result that if the characteristic functions of X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are holonomic (satisfy a linear homogeneous differential equation with polynomial coefficients) or if the density functions of X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are holonomic, then PSO⁡(X1)∩PSO⁡(X2)≠{0}\mathrm{PSO}(X_{1})\cap\mathrm{PSO}(X_{2})\not=\{0\} (see Theorem 5.1). From a probabilistic point of view this result may seem surprising, but it is in fact a consequence of basic properties of Weyl algebras. This demonstrates the power of the connection between Stein’s method and noncommutative algebra, and in this paper we have likely only scratched the surface of what can be achieved through this connection. We hope this paper inspires both probabilists and algebraists to further explore this seemingly fruitful new window on Stein’s method.

Remark 1.3 (Note on the class of functions ℱ\mathcal{F} II).

We require that the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is invariant under any polynomial differential operator, that is to say S​ℱ⊆ℱS\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{F} for any differential operator SS with polynomial coefficients. For probabilistic purposes, the following natural choices for function space ℱ\mathcal{F} are available: (a) ℱ=ℝ⁡[x]\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{R}[x] the ring of all polynomials with real coefficients; (b) ℱ=Cc∞​(ℝ)\mathcal{F}=C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}) the space of all infinitely differentiable functions with compact support; (c) the class of Schwartz functions ℱ=𝒮(ℝ):={f∈C∞(ℝ):supx∈ℝ|xα∂βf(x)|<∞,∀α,β∈ℕ0}\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}):=\{f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})\,:\,\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}f(x)|<\infty,\,\forall\,\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\}, which includes the class Cc∞​(ℝ)C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}); and (d) ℱ=P⁡(ℝ):={f∈C∞​(ℝ):supx∈ℝ|(1+xα)−1​∂βf⁡(x)|<∞​for all β∈ℕ0 and some α≥1}\mathcal{F}=P(\mathbb{R}):=\{f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})\,:\,\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|(1+x^{\alpha})^{-1}\partial^{\beta}f(x)|<\infty\,\text{for all $\beta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$ and some $\alpha\geq 1$}\} the space of infinitely differentiable functions with polynomial growth. Note that these families of functions are invariant under any polynomial differential operator. The Schwartz class ℱ=𝒮⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) is applicable to all target distributions. When target distributions have all moments (such as distributions in Wiener chaoses or probability distributions with bounded support), the classes ℱ=ℝ⁡[x]\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{R}[x] and ℱ=P⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{F}=P(\mathbb{R}) are also available. The class ℱ=ℝ⁡[x]\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{R}[x] is of particular interest for target distributions that are moment-determined. It is classical that the standard Gaussian distribution is moment-determined; see e.g. [NP12, Lemma 3.1.]. The class ℱ=P⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{F}=P(\mathbb{R}) is useful in practical implementations of Stein’s method, containing the real and and imaginary parts of the function f⁡(x)=ei​t​xf(x)=e^{\mathrm{i}tx}, t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, and ensuring that, for ff in this class, I​E​|Xα​∂βf⁡(X)|<∞{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}|X^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}f(X)|<\infty for all α,β∈ℕ0\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, if XX has all moments. To keep the statements of our results concise, when considering an arbitrary target random variable, the shorthand notation PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) can be safely considered to represent PSOℱ​(X)\text{PSO}_{\mathcal{F}}(X), where ℱ=𝒮⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}). However, if all moments of the target random variable(s) exist (as is the case for the Gaussian distribution), then the results also apply for ℱ=ℝ⁡[x]\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{R}[x], ℱ=P⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{F}=P(\mathbb{R}), and the class ℱS,Y\mathcal{F}_{S,Y} defined in Remark 1.2.

2 Auxiliary background

2.1 Elements of Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K})

In this section, we collect some relevant basic definitions and results from noncommutative algebra; for a comprehensive treatment of the subject, the reader can consult the classical textbooks [MR87, CF08, GW04, Lam01]. We begin by recalling some definitions from ring theory, which will be used throughout this paper. We then introduce some basic theory for Weyl algebras and holonomic functions that will be required in this paper. Throughout this section, 𝕂\mathbb{K} denotes a commutative field of characteristic zero. For our purposes, either 𝕂=ℝ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}, or 𝕂=ℂ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C} (the field of complex numbers).

Definition 2.1 (Ring).

A ring is a triplet (R,+,⋅)(R,+,\cdot) in which RR is a non-empty set equipped with two binary operations ++ and ⋅\cdot called addition and multiplication, respectively, such that:

  • (i)

    (R,+)(R,+) is an abelian group.

  • (ii)

    (R,⋅)(R,\cdot) is a monoid.

  • (iii)

    Addition and multiplication are related to each other via distributive laws: (a+b)⋅c=a⋅b+b⋅c(a+b)\cdot c=a\cdot b+b\cdot c and a⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅ca\cdot(b+c)=a\cdot b+a\cdot c.

The neutral element of RR under the addition operator is called zero and denoted by 0R=00_{R}=0, whereas the neutral element under the multiplication operator is called one or the unit-element and is denoted by 1R=11_{R}=1. The inverse of an element a∈Ra\in R under the addition operator is denoted by −a-a, i.e., a+(−a)=0a+(-a)=0. The ring RR is called commutative if a⋅b=b⋅aa\cdot b=b\cdot a for all a,b∈Ra,b\in R, and otherwise we say RR is noncommutative. We often omit the multiplication sign and write a​bab instead of a⋅ba\cdot b.

Definition 2.2 (Ideal).

A left (right) ideal II of a ring RR is a subgroup of (R,+)(R,+) such that R​I⊆IRI\subseteq I (I​R⊆I)(IR\subseteq I). We also write I⊲lRI\lhd_{l}R and I⊲rRI\lhd_{r}R to denote a left/right ideal. A two-sided ideal II – often referred to simply as an ideal – is a left and right ideal simultaneously, that is R​I⊆IRI\subseteq I and I​R⊆IIR\subseteq I. We denote it by I⊲RI\lhd R.

We now recall a number of further fundamental concepts from ring theory:

Definition 2.3.

Let RR be a ring (not necessarily commutative).

  • (a)

    The ring RR is an integral domain if the product of two non-zero elements is non-zero, i.e., a​b≠0ab\neq 0 for every 0≠a,b∈R0\neq a,b\in R.

  • (b)

    The ring RR is simple if 00 and RR are the only two-sided ideals of RR.

  • (c)

    The ring RR is a principal left (right) ideal ring if every left (right) ideal is principal (or generated by only one element).

  • (d)

    A left (right) ideal I⊲lRI\lhd_{l}R (I⊲rRI\lhd_{r}R) is called maximal if there is no left (right) proper ideal JJ containing II.

  • (e)

    The ring RR is prime if for every 0≠a,b∈R0\neq a,b\in R then a​R​b≠0aRb\neq 0. A left (right) ideal I⊲lRI\lhd_{l}R (I⊲rRI\lhd_{r}R) is called a prime ideal if the quotient R/IR/I is a prime ring.

  • (f)

    The ring RR is called left (right) Noetherian if it satisfies the left (right) ascending chain condition, namely that every chain of left (right) ideals I1⊆I2⊆I3⊆⋯I_{1}\subseteq I_{2}\subseteq I_{3}\subseteq\cdots must terminate after a finite step, i.e., there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that In=In+1=⋯I_{n}=I_{n+1}=\cdots.

A further fundamental concept from ring theory that will be needed in this paper is that of modules.

Definition 2.4 (Module).

Let RR be a ring (not necessarily commutative). An abelian group (M,+)(M,+) is called a left RR-module if there is a mapping ∙:R×M→M\bullet:R\times M\to M such that for all a,b∈Ra,b\in R and for all m,m′∈Mm,m^{\prime}\in M:

  • (i)

    a∙(m+m′)=a∙m+a∙m′a\bullet(m+m^{\prime})=a\bullet m+a\bullet m^{\prime}.

  • (ii)

    (a+b)∙m=a∙m+b∙m(a+b)\bullet m=a\bullet m+b\bullet m.

  • (iii)

    (a​b)∙m=a∙(b∙m)(ab)\bullet m=a\bullet(b\bullet m).

  • (iv)

    1∙m=m1\bullet m=m, where 1=1R1=1_{R}.

In brief, we write MR{}_{R}M to say MM is a left RR-module. A right RR-module is defined similarly, and denoted by MRM_{R}. A left RR-module MR{}_{R}M is said to be finitely generated if there is a finite set X={xi:i∈I}⊆MX=\{x_{i}\,:\,i\in I\}\subseteq M, say of the cardinality |I|=n|I|=n, so that for every element m∈Mm\in M there are a1,…,an∈Ra_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\in R such that m=a1∙x1+…+an∙xnm=a_{1}\bullet x_{1}+\ldots+a_{n}\bullet x_{n}. In this case we write MR=⟨X⟩R=⟨x1,…,xn⟩R{}_{R}M={}_{R}\langle X\rangle={}_{R}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle. If n=1n=1, that is when MR{}_{R}M is generated by only one element, it is called a cyclic module.

Example 2.1.

(a) Let RR be a ring. Every left ideal I⊲lRI\lhd_{l}R with the ring multiplication is a left RR-module. Similarly, every right ideal I⊲rRI\lhd_{r}R with the ring multiplication is a right RR-module. (b) Let a1,…,an∈Ra_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\in R. Then ⟨a1,…,an⟩R=∑i=1nRai={∑i=1nriai:ri∈R, 1≤i≤n}{}_{R}\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}Ra_{i}=\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}r_{i}a_{i}\,:\,r_{i}\in R,\,1\leq i\leq n\} is a finitely generated left RR-module.

Before moving on to some basic theory for Weyl algebras and holonomic functions we introduce the notion of an annihilator of a subset of a module over a ring, which will be used throughout this paper and also in our definition of holonomic functions later in this section.

Definition 2.5 (Annihilator).

Let MR{}_{R}M be a left RR-module. Let X⊆MX\subseteq M be a subset of MM. The annihilator of XX, denoted by AnnR​(X)\mathrm{Ann}_{R}(X), consists of those elements r∈Rr\in R such that for all elements x∈Xx\in X, r∙x=0r\bullet x=0. In set notation,

AnnR​(X)={r∈R:r∙x=0​∀x∈X}.\mathrm{Ann}_{R}(X)=\{r\in R\,:\,r\bullet x=0\,\,\forall\,x\in X\}.

We are now ready to define the Weyl algebra.

Definition 2.6 (Weyl algebras).

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} be a natural number. The nnth Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) is an associative 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra (a vector space over the field 𝕂\mathbb{K} equipped with a bilinear operator which is associative, that is to say r⁡(a⋅b)=(r​a)⋅b=a⋅(r​b)r(a\cdot b)=(ra)\cdot b=a\cdot(rb) for every r∈𝕂r\in\mathbb{K} and every a,b∈An​(𝕂)a,b\in A_{n}(\mathbb{K})) with generators xn,…,xnx_{n},\ldots,x_{n}, y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} subject to the relations

[xi,xj]=[yi,yj]=0,[xi,yj]=δi​j,∀ 1≤i,j≤n,[x_{i},x_{j}]=[y_{i},y_{j}]=0,\quad[x_{i},y_{j}]=\delta_{ij},\quad\forall\,1\leq i,j\leq n,

where [a,b]=a​b−b​a[a,b]=ab-ba is the commutator of the elements aa and bb, and δi​j\delta_{ij} denotes the Kronecker delta. Let 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be the ring of polynomials in nn variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} with coefficients in 𝕂\mathbb{K}. It is classical that the nnth Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) is isomorphic (as a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-algebra) to the ring of differential operators with polynomial coefficients in nn variables by identifying each yiy_{i} with ∂i=∂xi\partial_{i}=\partial_{x_{i}}. Clearly, An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) is a noncommutative ring.

The following theorem (see [MR87, Theorem 1.15]) collects some algebraic properties of Weyl algebras. The right Ore property described in part (b) of Theorem 2.1 will allow us to provide an efficient proof of Theorem 5.1 that concerns the non-characterising nature of classes of polynomial Stein operators.

Theorem 2.1.
  • (a)

    The Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) is a simple Noetherian (left/right) integral domain, and hence is a prime ring.

  • (b)

    The Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) satisfies the left/right Ore property, namely that An​(𝕂)​L∩An​(𝕂)​S≠{0}A_{n}(\mathbb{K})L\cap A_{n}(\mathbb{K})S\neq\{0\} for every two non-zero elements L,S∈An​(𝕂)L,S\in A_{n}(\mathbb{K}).

In order to formulate some further fundamental results on Weyl algebras we will require the following definitions.

Definition 2.7.
  • (a)

    (Bernstein filtration). Let ν∈ℕ0\nu\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. Let ℱν\mathscr{F}_{\nu} be a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space which is generated by elements {xα∂β:|α|+|β|≤ν}\{x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\,:\,|\alpha|+|\beta|\leq\nu\}, where for a multi-index α=(α1,…,αn)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}) we let |α|=∑i=1nαi|\alpha|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}. Clearly, each ℱν\mathscr{F}_{\nu} is a finite dimensional 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space, ℱ0⊂ℱ1⊂⋯\mathscr{F}_{0}\subset\mathscr{F}_{1}\subset\cdots, ∪ν=0∞ℱν=An(𝕂)\cup_{\nu=0}^{\infty}\mathscr{F}_{\nu}=A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) and ℱν​ℱk⊂ℱν+k\mathscr{F}_{\nu}\mathscr{F}_{k}\subset\mathscr{F}_{\nu+k}. The family ℱ={ℱν:ν≥0}\mathscr{F}=\{\mathscr{F}_{\nu}\,:\,\nu\geq 0\} is called the Bernstein filtration for the Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}). The direct sum gr⁡(An​(𝕂)):=ℱ0⊕ℱ1ℱ0⊕ℱ2ℱ1⊕⋯\mathrm{gr}\left(A_{n}(\mathbb{K})\right):=\mathscr{F}_{0}\oplus\frac{\mathscr{F}_{1}}{\mathscr{F}_{0}}\oplus\frac{\mathscr{F}_{2}}{\mathscr{F}_{1}}\oplus\cdots is called the associated graded ring.

  • (b)

    (Good filtration). Let MM be a left An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K})-module. A filtration Γ=(Γν:ν≥0)\Gamma=(\Gamma_{\nu}\,:\,\nu\geq 0) is an increasing sequence of finite dimensional vector subspaces on 𝕂\mathbb{K} such that M=∪ν=0∞ΓνM=\cup_{\nu=0}^{\infty}\Gamma_{\nu} and ℱk​Γν⊂Γν+k\mathscr{F}_{k}\Gamma_{\nu}\subset\Gamma_{\nu+k} for every pair kk and ν\nu. For a given filtration Γ\Gamma, the associated graded gr​(An​(𝕂))\mathrm{gr}\left(A_{n}(\mathbb{K})\right)-module is given as grΓ​M:=Γ0⊕Γ1Γ0⊕Γ2Γ1⊕⋯\mathrm{gr}_{\Gamma}M:=\Gamma_{0}\oplus\frac{\Gamma_{1}}{\Gamma_{0}}\oplus\frac{\Gamma_{2}}{\Gamma_{1}}\oplus\cdots. A filtration Γ\Gamma is called a good filtration if the associated graded grΓ​M\mathrm{gr}_{\Gamma}M is a finitely generated graded gr​(An​(𝕂))\mathrm{gr}\left(A_{n}(\mathbb{K})\right)-module.

  • (c)

    (Bernstein dimension). Let Γ\Gamma be a good filtration on a finitely generated left An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K})-module MM. Then, it is well-known that there is d≥0d\geq 0 and rational numbers a0,…,ada_{0},\ldots,a_{d} so that dimK​Γν=ad​νd+⋯+a0\mathrm{dim}_{K}\Gamma_{\nu}=a_{d}\nu^{d}+\cdots+a_{0} for ν≫0\nu\gg 0. The integer d=:dΓ​(M)=d⁡(M)d=:d_{\Gamma}(M)=d(M) is called the Bernstein dimension, and it is well-known that dd is independent of the choice of good filtration.

  • (d)

    (Holonomic module). A finitely generated left An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K})-module MM is called a holonomic module if d⁡(M)=nd(M)=n. It is well-known that for every non-zero finitely generated left An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K})-module MM it holds d⁡(M)≥nd(M)\geq n. This is known as Bernstein’s inequality.

In studying the algebraic structure of PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) in Section 3.2 we will employ the following fundamental results.

Theorem 2.2 (Stafford’s theorems).
  • (a)

    Every left (right) ideal in the nnth Weyl algebra An​(𝕂)A_{n}(\mathbb{K}) may be generated by two elements – see e.g. [Sta78, Theorem 3.1].

  • (b)

    Every holonomic AnA_{n}-module is cyclic, i.e. generated by one element – see e.g. [Cou95, Corollary 2.6].

The following example sets the scene for our brief review of relevant results from Holonomic function theory.

Example 2.2.

Let M=C∞​(𝕂)M=C^{\infty}(\mathbb{K}) be the vector space of infinitely many differentiable functions over the field 𝕂\mathbb{K}. Define the mapping ∙:A1​(𝕂)×M→M\bullet:A_{1}(\mathbb{K})\times M\to M, where the action of L=∑t=0Tpt∂tL=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t} on ff is defined by L∙f=∑t=0Tpt​∂tfL\bullet f=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}f. Recall that the coefficients ptp_{t}, t=0,1,…,Tt=0,1,\ldots,T, are polynomials in one variable. It is straightforward to see that MA1​(𝕂){}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{K})}M is a left A1​(𝕂)A_{1}(\mathbb{K})-module.

2.2 Holonomic functions

We begin by stating a definition of holonomic functions, making use of the terminology built up in this section. For an introduction to holonomic function theory the reader is referred to the excellent textbooks [Sta98, FS09].

Definition 2.8 (Holonomic function).

A function f:Dom⁡(f)⊆𝕂→𝕂f:{\rm{Dom}}(f)\subseteq\mathbb{K}\to\mathbb{K} is called holonomic (or ∂\partial-finite, or DD-finite) if it satisfies one of the following equivalent conditions:

  • (a)

    AnnA1​(𝕂)​(f):={L∈A1​(𝕂):L∙f=0}≠{0}\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{K})}(f):=\{L\in A_{1}(\mathbb{K})\,:\,L\bullet f=0\}\neq\{0\}.

  • (b)

    The vector space spanned by (∂tf:t=0,1,…)(\partial^{t}f:t=0,1,\ldots) is finite dimensional over the field of rational functions 𝕂(x)={p⁡(x)q⁡(x):p,q∈𝕂[x]}\mathbb{K}(x)=\big\{\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\,:\,p,q\in\mathbb{K}[x]\big\} with the usual addition and multiplication operations on polynomials.

The class of holonomic functions enjoys rich closure properties. The following result is borrowed from [FS09, Theorem B2] and [FGS05, Theorem 1]. These closure properties can allow for efficient proofs that given functions are holonomic when a direct application of the definition is not tractable, a point which is illustrated in our proof of Proposition 3.2 that relies on the closure properties of holonomic functions.

Theorem 2.3.

(a) The class of univariate holonomic functions is closed under the following mathematical operations: (i) sum, (ii) product, (iii) differentiation, (iv) indefinite integration, and (v) algebraic substitution.

(b) A holonomic function has only finitely many singularities.

(c) If the function f⁡(x1,…,xn)f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) is holonomic, then, for any aa and bb, the function given by ∫abf⁡(x1,…,xn−1,xn)​d​xn\int_{a}^{b}f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1},x_{n})\,dx_{n} is also holonomic, if it is defined ([Zei90, Proposition 3.5]).

From Theorem 2.3, we know that a holonomic function possesses only finitely many singularities. The asymptotic behaviour of a holonomic functions in a neighbourhood of one of its singularities is described by the following theorem.

Theorem 2.4 (see [Was65] Theorem 19.1, [FGS05] Theorem 2).

Let f:Dom⁡(f)⊆ℝ→ℝf:{\rm{Dom}}(f)\subseteq\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be a holonomic function satisfying the ordinary differential equation (ODE)

∑t=0Tpt​∂tf⁡(x)=0.\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}f(x)=0. (2.1)

Let x0x_{0} be a singular point of ff. Then there exists a sufficiently small neighborhood of x0x_{0} such that the following asymptotic expansion holds:

f(x)∼exp(P(x−x0)−1/r)(x−x0)α∑j=0∞Qj(log(x−x0))(x−x0)j​β,x→x0,f(x)\sim\exp\left(P\left(x-x_{0}\right)^{-1/r}\right)(x-x_{0})^{\alpha}\,\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}Q_{j}(\log(x-x_{0}))(x-x_{0})^{j\beta},\quad x\to x_{0},

where PP is a polynomial, r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}, β∈ℚ>0\beta\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}, and the QjQ_{j} are a family of polynomials of uniformly bounded degree. The choice of the quantities P,Qj,r,α,βP,Q_{j},r,\alpha,\beta depends upon the particular solution of the ODE (2.1).

Let L=∑t=0Tpt∂tL=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t} be a linear differential operator with polynomial coefficients. The algebraic (or formal) adjoint of LL is defined as

L∗​f:=∑t=0T(−1)t​∂t(pt​f).L^{*}f:=\sum_{t=0}^{T}(-1)^{t}\partial^{t}(p_{t}\,f). (2.2)

It is classical [Inc56, page 211] that the operator LL and its algebraic adjoint L∗L^{*} are linked together by the so-called Lagrange identity: for sufficiently regular f,gf,g,

g​L​f−f​L∗​g=∂∂x​PL​(f,g),gLf-fL^{*}g=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}P_{L}(f,g), (2.3)

where PL​(f,g)P_{L}(f,g) is the bilinear concomitant, a homogeneous bilinear form which can be written explicitly as

PL​(f,g)\displaystyle P_{L}(f,g) =f⁡{p1​g−∂(p2​g)+⋯+(−1)T−1​∂T−1(pT​g)}\displaystyle=f\Big\{p_{1}g-\partial(p_{2}g)+\cdots+(-1)^{T-1}\partial^{T-1}(p_{T}g)\Big\} (2.4)
+f′​{p2​g−∂(p3​g)+⋯+(−1)T−2​∂T−2(pT​g)}\displaystyle+f^{\prime}\Big\{p_{2}g-\partial(p_{3}g)+\cdots+(-1)^{T-2}\partial^{T-2}(p_{T}g)\Big\}
⋮\displaystyle\vdots

The Green’s formula is obtained by taking integration over the interval (a,b)⊆ℝ(a,b)\subseteq\mathbb{R} (where −∞≤a<b≤∞-\infty\leq a<b\leq\infty) of both sides of (2.3):

∫abg⁡(x)​L​f​(x)​𝑑x−∫abf⁡(x)​L∗​g​(x)​𝑑x=PL​(f⁡(x),g⁡(x))|ab\int_{a}^{b}g(x)Lf(x)\,dx-\int_{a}^{b}f(x)L^{*}g(x)\,dx=P_{L}(f(x),g(x))\,\Big|_{a}^{b} (2.5)

whenever the integrals exist.

2.3 A gentle introduction to Malliavin operators

For the scope of our paper, it is enough to define Malliavin operators in dimension d=1d=1 algebraically, without discussing their functional analytic extensions. For a state-of-the-art exposition of Malliavin calculus in full generality see [NP12, NN18].

Definition 2.9.

In the univariate case, the Malliavin derivative DD, the divergence δ\delta and its pseudo-inverse δ−1\delta^{-1} are defined as linear mappings acting on the polynomial ring ℝ⁡[x]\mathbb{R}[x], with

Dxn=∂xn=nxn−1,δxn=(x−∂)xn=xn+1−nxn−1,and\displaystyle Dx^{n}=\partial x^{n}=nx^{n-1},\quad\delta x^{n}=(x-\partial)x^{n}=x^{n+1}-nx^{n-1},\quad\text{and}

where n!!n!\!! denotes the double factorial. Also, it holds that δ−1​δ​xn=xn\delta^{-1}\delta x^{n}=x^{n}, and δ​δ−1​xn=xn−I​E​[Xn]\delta\delta^{-1}x^{n}=x^{n}-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[X^{n}\right], with X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1), where the standard Gaussian distribution has moment sequence I​E​[Xn]=(n−1)!!{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[X^{n}\right]=(n-1)!\!! when n∈2​ℕn\in 2\mathbb{N} and I​E​[Xn]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[X^{n}\right]=0 otherwise.

Let p≥2p\geq 2. We define the ppth Malliavin derivative and divergence operators as follows: Dp​f=∂pf=f(p)D^{p}f=\partial^{p}f=f^{(p)}, and δp​f=δ⁡(δp−1​f)=δp−1​(δ​f)\delta^{p}f=\delta\left(\delta^{p-1}f\right)=\delta^{p-1}(\delta f).

Proposition 2.1 (Gaussian integration by parts).

Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). For f,g∈ℝ⁡[x]f,g\in\mathbb{R}[x],

I​E​[f⁡(X)​D​g​(X)]=I​E​[f⁡(X)​∂g⁡(X)]=I​E​[g⁡(X)​δ​f​(X)].\displaystyle{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[f(X)Dg(X)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[f(X)\partial g(X)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[g(X)\delta f(X)\bigr]. (2.6)

Hermite polynomials play a fundamental role in Malliavin calculus. For our purposes, it will suffice to provide the following definition of the Hermite polynomials that employs the divergence operator, along with the forthcoming fact that any every polynomial can be written as a finite sum of Hermite polynomials. Many further properties can be found in the books [NP12, NN18].

Definition 2.10 (Hermite polynomials).

We define the univariate Hermite polynomials as H0​(x)=1H_{0}(x)=1 and

Hn​(x)=δ​Hn−1​(x)=(δn​1)​(x),n≥1.H_{n}(x)=\delta H_{n-1}(x)=\bigl(\delta^{n}1\bigr)(x),\quad n\geq 1.

Proposition 2.2.

H0​(x),…,Hn​(x)H_{0}(x),\dots,H_{n}(x) are monic polynomials spanning ℝn​[x]\mathbb{R}_{n}[x] (the ring of polynomials of maximum degree nn).

For a given (target) polynomial y=h⁡(x)y=h(x), with h∈ℝ⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{R}[x], we introduce the linear operator Γy\Gamma_{y} acting on ℝ⁡[x]\mathbb{R}[x] as

=I​E​[∂(g∘h)​(X)​δ−1​f​(X)]=I​E​[∂g⁡(Y)​ΓY​(f⁡(X))].\displaystyle={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[\partial(g\circ h)(X)\delta^{-1}f(X)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[\partial g(Y)\Gamma_{Y}(f(X))\bigr].

3 Algebraic structure of classes of polynomial Stein operators

3.1 General results and a connection between Stein’s method and holonomic function theory

We open this section with a general result on the algebraic structure of PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X), the class of polynomial Stein operators of a given continuous target random variable XX. Parts (a) and (b) make a connection between Stein’s method and holonomic function theory, and provide simple conditions under which the class PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) is non-trivial, that is PSO⁡(X)≠{0}\mathrm{PSO}(X)\neq\{0\}. In the forthcoming Remark 3.1, Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.1, we will apply Proposition 3.1 in some concrete settings. Parts (c) of Proposition 3.1 tells us that for a given continuous target random variable XX, the class PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) can be generated by at most two polynomial Stein operators for XX, whilst part (d) gives an initial simple result on the question of whether PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) is principal. We consider the matter of whether PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) is principal to be important, and will consider this questions in the concrete settings that X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1) in Section 3.2 and X=Hp​(N)X=H_{p}(N) in Section 3.3.

Proposition 3.1.
  • (a)

    Let φX\varphi_{X} denote the characteristic function of the random variable XX. Then AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φX)≠{0}\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{X})\neq\{0\} if and only if φX\varphi_{X} is holonomic. In addition, PSO⁡(X)≠{0}\mathrm{PSO}(X)\neq\{0\} if and only if AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φX)≠{0}\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{X})\neq\{0\}.

  • (b)

    Let XX be an absolutely continuous random variable with probability density function given by pX​(x)=d​FX​(x)d​xp_{X}(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}F_{X}(x)}{\mathrm{d}x}, where FXF_{X} denotes the cumulative distribution function of XX. Then, PSO⁡(X)≠{0}\mathrm{PSO}(X)\neq\{0\} if and only if pXp_{X} is holonomic.

  • (c)

    PSO(X)⊲rA1(ℝ)\mathrm{PSO}(X)\lhd_{r}A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) is a right ideal of the first Weyl algebra A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}). Moreover, PSO⁡(X)\mathrm{PSO}(X) can be generated by two elements, i.e. PSO⁡(X)=⟨G1,G2⟩A1​(ℝ)\mathrm{PSO}(X)=\langle G_{1},G_{2}\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})} for some G1,G2∈A1​(ℝ)G_{1},G_{2}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}).

  • (d)

    PSO⁡(X)\mathrm{PSO}(X) is a right principal ideal if and only if AnnA1​(ℂ)(φX)⊲lA1(ℂ)\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{X})\lhd_{l}A_{1}(\mathbb{C}) is a left principal ideal in the first Weyl algebra A1​(ℂ)A_{1}(\mathbb{C}).

We will need the following lemma in our proof of Proposition 3.1.

Lemma 3.1.

The Fourier operator Ψ:A1​(ℂ)→A1​(ℂ)\Psi:A_{1}(\mathbb{C})\to A_{1}(\mathbb{C}), given by

xn∂xk↦Ψ(xn∂xk)=ik−ntk∂tn,k,n∈ℕ0,\displaystyle x^{n}\partial_{x}^{k}\mapsto\Psi\bigl(x^{n}\partial_{x}^{k})=\mathrm{i}^{k-n}t^{k}\partial_{t}^{n},\quad k,n\in\mathbb{N}_{0},

extended by linearity is an anti-isomorphism of the Weyl algebra A1​(ℂ)A_{1}(\mathbb{C}), that is to say, a bijection so that for every S1,S2∈A1​(ℂ)S_{1},S_{2}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C}),

Ψ⁡(S1​S2)=Ψ⁡(S2)​Ψ​(S1).\displaystyle\Psi(S_{1}S_{2})=\Psi(S_{2})\Psi(S_{1}).
Proof.

Clearly, Ψ\Psi is a bijective map. On the other hand, the set {xn∂xk:n,k∈ℕ0}\{x^{n}\partial^{k}_{x}\,:\,n,k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\} provides a basis (as a vector space) over the field ℂ\mathbb{C}; see [Bjö79, Proposition 1.2]. Therefore, since

and

Remark 3.1.

(a) Many continuous probability distributions admit holonomic characteristic functions, including the Gaussian, exponential, gamma, beta, variance-gamma, Pearson distributions, and semicircular just to mention a few. Therefore, according to Proposition 3.1 part (a), the associated polynomial Stein operator classes are non-trivial; indeed, polynomial Stein operators are known for all these distributions as well as many others; we refer the reader to [AGG23a, GMS19, LRS17] and references therein for an overview of this literature.

(b) Let XX follow the extreme value Gumbel distribution with density function pX​(x)=e−x​e−e−xp_{X}(x)=e^{-x}e^{-e^{-x}}, x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. All moments of the Gumbel distribution exist. It is known that the characteristic function is given by φX​(t)=Γ⁡(1−i​t)\varphi_{X}(t)=\Gamma(1-\mathrm{i}t), where the gamma function is defined by Γ⁡(z)=∫0∞xz−1​e−x​𝑑x\Gamma(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{z-1}e^{-x}\,dx, for Re​(z)>0\text{Re}(z)>0. The gamma function Γ⁡(z)\Gamma(z) is not a holonomic function, see, e.g., [Kau13, p. 4], and therefore the characteristic function φX\varphi_{X} is not holonomic. Therefore, PSO​(X)=0\text{PSO}(X)=0 is the trivial ideal. For Gumbel approximation via Stein’s method the reader can consult [LRS17, CF16].

(c) Let XX follow the log-normal distribution with density function given by pX(x)=(2π)−1/2x−1exp(−(log(x))2/2)p_{X}(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}x^{-1}\exp(-(\log(x))^{2}/2), x>0x>0. All moments of the log-normal distribution exist. It is readily seen that pX​(x)p_{X}(x) is not a holonomic function [FGS05], and therefore PSO⁡(X)={0}\mathrm{PSO}(X)=\{0\} is the trivial ideal. A brief account of the Malliavin-Stein method for log-normal approximation is given by [KT12]. We also remark that it is a well-known open problem to find a closed-form expression for the characteristic function of the log-normal distribution. Proposition 3.1 tells us that the characteristic function of the log-normal distribution is not holonomic and thus does not satisfy a homogeneous, linear ordinary differential equation with rational coefficients. This partially explains the difficulty in finding a closed-form formula for the characteristic function, because many of the standard special functions are solutions of homogeneous, linear ODEs with rational coefficients.

From Proposition 3.1 and the closure properties of holonomic functions, we deduce the following proposition which shows that the class of polynomial Stein operators for a wide family of distributions is non-trivial.

Proposition 3.2.

Suppose h∈ℝ⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{R}[x] (the ring of polynomials with real-valued coefficients) and let XX be a real-valued random variable with holonomic density. Let Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X). Then PSO⁡(Y)≠{0}\mathrm{PSO}(Y)\not=\{0\}.

As the Gaussian density is holonomic, the following corollary is immediate. This answers one of the open problems raised by our recent work [AGG23a].

Corollary 3.1.

Let N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). Then, for any h∈ℝ⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{R}[x], we have PSO⁡(h⁡(N))≠{0}\mathrm{PSO}(h(N))\not=\{0\}.

Proof of Proposition 3.2. Suppose without loss of generality that h∈ℝ⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{R}[x] has k≥0k\geq 0 distinct local maxima and minima, which we label by y1<y2<⋯<yky_{1}<y_{2}<\cdots<y_{k}. Suppose that the support of Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) is given by the interval (a,b)∈ℝ(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}, and for ease of notation define y0:=ay_{0}:=a and yk+1:=by_{k+1}:=b. Suppose y∈(yi,yi+1)y\in(y_{i},y_{i+1}) for 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k. Then, the density of the random variable Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) can be expressed as

fY​(y)=∑h⁡(x)=yfX​(x)|h′​(x)|.\displaystyle f_{Y}(y)=\sum_{h(x)=y}\frac{f_{X}(x)}{|h^{\prime}(x)|}.

From the closure properties of holonomic functions (see Theorem 2.3), we may now argue that the density of YY is holonomic. We have that y↦xyy\mapsto x_{y}, a solution of h⁡(xy)=yh(x_{y})=y, is holonomic, as the equation is algebraic. Also, g=1/h′g=1/h^{\prime} is holonomic, as it satisfies the ODE (h′​(x))2​g′​(x)+h′′​(x)=0(h^{\prime}(x))^{2}g^{\prime}(x)+h^{\prime\prime}(x)=0. Thus, by composition, y↦1/h′​(xy)y\mapsto 1/h^{\prime}(x_{y}) is holonomic. By the same reasoning, y↦fX​(xy)y\mapsto f_{X}(x_{y}) is holonomic (by assumption fXf_{X} is holonomic), and by product fX​(xy)/|h′​(xy)|f_{X}(x_{y})/|h^{\prime}(x_{y})| is holonomic. Thus, we have shown that the density fYf_{Y} is holonomic on each of the intervals (yi,yi+1)(y_{i},y_{i+1}), 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k.

To conclude that fYf_{Y} is holonomic over its whole support, we make use of a classical fact that the ring of linear differential operators with polynomial coefficients is a left Euclidean domain [Ore33]. By the discussion above, we can write fY​(y)=∑i=0kfi​(y)​1{(yi,yi+1)}​(y)f_{Y}(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}f_{i}(y)\textbf{1}_{\{(y_{i},y_{i+1})\}}(y), where each fif_{i} is holonomic. Let 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k and assume that 0≠Li∈A1​(ℝ)0\neq L_{i}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) annihilates the density function fYf_{Y} over the interval (yi,yi+1)(y_{i},y_{i+1}). Denote by LL the least common left divisor of L1,…,LkL_{1},\ldots,L_{k}. Note that L≠0L\neq 0 and clearly the operator S=∏i=0k(y−yi)ord⁡(L)​LS=\prod_{i=0}^{k}(y-y_{i})^{\mathrm{ord}(L)}L annihilates the entire density function fYf_{Y} where here ord⁡(L)\mathrm{ord}(L) stands for the order of the operator LL (it is known that ord⁡(L)≤∑iord⁡(Li)\mathrm{ord}(L)\leq\sum_{i}\mathrm{ord}(L_{i}), see [BCLS, Theorem 6]). The result now follows by part (b) of Proposition 3.1. □\Box

3.2 Algebraic structure of PSO(NN)

Our description of the algebraic structure of PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) is given in the following theorem.

Theorem 3.1.

Consider PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N), the class of all polynomial Stein operators associated to the standard Gaussian random variable NN. Then the following statements are in order:

  • (a)

    PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a vector space over ℝ\mathbb{R} with basis

    𝔅:={S(k,t):=Hk∂t−Hk+t,k,t∈ℕ0}.\displaystyle\mathbf{\mathfrak{B}}:=\Big\{S(k,t):=H_{k}\partial^{t}-H_{k+t},\quad k,t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\Big\}. (3.3)
  • (b)

    PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a principal maximal right ideal, and

    PSO⁡(N)=⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ)=G​A1​(ℝ):={G​L:L∈A1​(ℝ)},\mathrm{PSO}(N)=\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})}=GA_{1}(\mathbb{R}):=\big\{GL\,:\,L\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R})\big\}, (3.4)

    where the generator G=∂−xG=\partial-x. (Equivalently, the ideal PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N), as a module on the first Weyl algebra A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}), is a cyclic module.)

  • (c)

    The ideal PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) (as a A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) module) is not holonomic, although the quotient A1​(ℝ)/PSO​(N)A_{1}(\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a holonomic module. In addition, d⁡(A1​(ℝ)/PSO⁡(N))=1d(A_{1}(\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{PSO}(N))=1 and d⁡(PSO⁡(N))=2d(\mathrm{PSO}(N))=2.

Remark 3.2.
  • (a)

    The first Weyl algebra A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) is not a principal ideal domain. In fact, the ideal generated by elements x2x^{2} and 1+x∂1+x\partial is not principal, see [MR87, Example 7.11.8].

  • (b)

    Items (b)-(c) of Theorem 3.1 reveal that PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) is a cyclic non-holonomic module on the first Weyl algebra A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}). It is a well-known fact in DD-module theory that every holonomic module is cyclic; see Theorem 2.2 item (b).

Remark 3.3.

Consider the right ideal I=⟨G⟩⊲rA1(ℝ)I=\langle G\rangle\lhd_{r}A_{1}(\mathbb{R}), where G=∂−xG=\partial-x. Clearly, I⊆PSO​(N)I\subseteq\text{PSO}(N). The quotient ideal A1​(ℝ)/IA_{1}(\mathbb{R})/I is a holonomic module (see e.g. [Cou95, p. 86]) and by part (b) of Stafford’s Theorem 2.2 is cyclic meaning that there is G′∈A1​(ℝ)G^{\prime}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) so that A1​(ℝ)/I=⟨G′+I⟩A_{1}(\mathbb{R})/I=\langle G^{\prime}+I\rangle. Therefore, PSO​(N)=⟨G,G′⟩A1​(ℝ)\text{PSO}(N)=\langle G,G^{\prime}\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})}. However, Theorem 3.1 part (b) yields that the extra generator G′G^{\prime} is immaterial.

In proving part (b) of Theorem 3.1 we will make use of the following simple lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

Let G=∂−x∈A1(ℝ)G=\partial-x\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}). Then, for every k,l∈ℕ0k,l\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, it holds that

G(Hk∂l)=Hk∂l+1−Hk+1∂l.G(H_{k}\partial^{l})=H_{k}\partial^{l+1}-H_{k+1}\partial^{l}.
Proof.

By definition of the operator GG, we can write

G(Hk∂l)\displaystyle G(H_{k}\partial^{l}) =∂(Hk∂l)−xHk∂l=∂(Hk)∂l+Hk∂l+1−xHk∂l\displaystyle=\partial(H_{k}\partial^{l})-xH_{k}\partial^{l}=\partial(H_{k})\partial^{l}+H_{k}\partial^{l+1}-xH_{k}\partial^{l}
=Hk∂l+1−(xHk−∂Hk)∂l=Hk∂l+1−δ(Hk)∂l\displaystyle=H_{k}\partial^{l+1}-\left(xH_{k}-\partial H_{k}\right)\partial^{l}=H_{k}\partial^{l+1}-\delta(H_{k})\partial^{l}
=Hk∂l+1−Hk+1∂l,\displaystyle=H_{k}\partial^{l+1}-H_{k+1}\partial^{l},

where we used Definition 2.10 of Hermite polynomials. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

(a) It is clear that PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) is a linear space. Now let S=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈A1(ℝ)S=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}). Observe that by using the Gaussian integration by parts formula (2.6), S∈PSO​(N)S\in\text{PSO}(N) if and only if

p0=−∑t=1Tδtpt.p_{0}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta^{t}p_{t}.

On the other hand, every polynomial can be written as a finite sum of Hermite polynomials; see Proposition 2.2. Hence, a basis of the linear space of Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution is given by the elements

S(k,t)=Hk∂t−δtHk=Hk∂t−Hk+t,t,k∈ℕ0.S(k,t)=H_{k}\partial^{t}-\delta^{t}H_{k}=H_{k}\partial^{t}-H_{k+t},\quad t,k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}.

(b) In order to show that PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) is a principal ideal, it is enough to show that for every element S⁡(k,t)∈𝔅S(k,t)\in\mathfrak{B} we have S⁡(k,t)=G​LS(k,t)=GL for some element L∈A1​(ℝ)L\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}). By taking telescoping sums and applying Lemma 3.2 in the second step,

S⁡(k,t)\displaystyle S(k,t) =−∑r=1t(Hk+t+1−r∂r−1−Hk+t−r∂r)=G(∑r=1tHk+t+1−r∂r−1).\displaystyle=-\sum_{r=1}^{t}\biggl(H_{k+t+1-r}\partial^{r-1}-H_{k+t-r}\partial^{r}\biggr)=G\biggl(\sum_{r=1}^{t}H_{k+t+1-r}\partial^{r-1}\biggr).

Maximality of PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) follows from [Lam01, Exercise 18, p. 50]. Maximality of principal ideals x​A1​(ℝ)xA_{1}(\mathbb{R}) and A1​(ℝ)​xA_{1}(\mathbb{R})x is also discussed in [MR87, p. 21].

(c) According to [Cou95], Corollary 1.2 and Proposition 1.3, Chapter 10, torsion and holonomic finitely generated A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) modules are the same thing. Now, if PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) were a holonomic module then this would imply that the generator G=∂−xG=\partial-x would be a torsion element, i.e., G​L=0GL=0 for some non-zero element L∈A1​(ℝ)L\in A_{1}(\mathbb{R}), which is a contradiction with A1​(ℝ)A_{1}(\mathbb{R}) being an integral domain. Lastly, the claim d​(PSO​(N))=2d(\text{PSO}(N))=2 follows directly from the Bernstein’s inequality. ∎

3.3 Algebraic structure of PSO(Hp​(N)H_{p}(N))

We begin this section by proving that the ideal PSO​(H2​(N))\text{PSO}(H_{2}(N)) is principle, where N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). In Proposition 3.3 below we shall then prove that the operator G=2(y+1)∂−y∈PSO(H2(N))G=2(y+1)\partial-y\in\text{PSO}(H_{2}(N)) is the generator of the ideal.

Example 3.1.

Let Y=H2​(N)=N2−1Y=H_{2}(N)=N^{2}-1, where N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). In this example, we show that the ideal PSO⁡(Y)\mathrm{PSO}(Y) is principal. Recall that the operator G=2(y+1)∂−y∈PSO(Y)G=2(y+1)\partial-y\in\mathrm{PSO}(Y). Let L=∑t=0Tpy(y)∂t∈PSO(Y)L=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{y}(y)\partial^{t}\in\mathrm{PSO}(Y) be arbitrary, where T≥2T\geq 2. I​E​[pT​(Y)​∂f⁡(Y)]=I​E​[δ⁡(pT​(Y)2​X)​f​(Y)].{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[p_{T}(Y)\partial f(Y)\right]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[\delta\left(\frac{p_{T}(Y)}{2X}\right)f(Y)\right].

Denote p0​(y):=δ⁡(pT​(y)2​x)p_{0}(y):=\delta(\frac{p_{T}(y)}{2x}), where here we have the association y=H2​(x)=x2−1y=H_{2}(x)=x^{2}-1. Hence, we are left to show that δ⁡(pT​(y)x)∈ℝ⁡[y]\delta(\frac{p_{T}(y)}{x})\in\mathbb{R}[y]. Now, from Proposition 4.1 [AGG23a], one can deduce that pT​(y)=(y+1)​h​(y)=x​t​(x)p_{T}(y)=(y+1)h(y)=xt(x) for some polynomials h⁡(y)∈ℝ⁡[y]h(y)\in\mathbb{R}[y], and t⁡(x)∈ℝ⁡[x]t(x)\in\mathbb{R}[x] (observe that pT​(y)/x∈ℝ⁡[x]p_{T}(y)/x\in\mathbb{R}[x]). Next, we have

δ(pT​(y)x)=(x−∂)(pT​(y)x)=pT(y)−∂x((y+1)​h​(y)x).\delta\bigg(\frac{p_{T}(y)}{x}\bigg)=\left(x-\partial\right)\left(\frac{p_{T}(y)}{x}\right)=p_{T}(y)-\partial_{x}\left(\frac{(y+1)h(y)}{x}\right).

Moreover,

∂x((y+1)​h​(y)x)\displaystyle\partial_{x}\left(\frac{(y+1)h(y)}{x}\right) =(2​x​h​(y)+2​x​(y+1)​h′​(y))​2​x−2​(y+1)​h​(y)4​x2\displaystyle=\frac{(2xh(y)+2x(y+1)h^{\prime}(y))2x-2(y+1)h(y)}{4x^{2}}
=12​h​(y)+(y+1)​h′​(y)∈ℝ⁡[y],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}h(y)+(y+1)h^{\prime}(y)\in\mathbb{R}[y],

and hence we are done.

Lemma 3.3.

Let Y=H2​(N)Y=H_{2}(N), where N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). Consider L=p0(y)+p1(y)∂L=p_{0}(y)+p_{1}(y)\partial with p0,p1∈ℝ⁡[y]p_{0},p_{1}\in\mathbb{R}[y], where we have identified y=H2​(x)=x2−1y=H_{2}(x)=x^{2}-1. Then

p0​(y)=−δ⁡((y+1)​h​(y)x)=−y​h​(y)+2​(y+1)​h′​(y).\displaystyle p_{0}(y)=-\delta\left(\frac{(y+1)h(y)}{x}\right)=-yh(y)+2(y+1)h^{\prime}(y).

L\displaystyle L =p0(y)+p1(y)∂=(−yh(y)+2(y+1)h′(y))+2(y+1)h(y)∂\displaystyle=p_{0}(y)+p_{1}(y)\partial=\left(-yh(y)+2(y+1)h^{\prime}(y)\right)+2(y+1)h(y)\partial
=G​h​(y)∈⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ).\displaystyle=Gh(y)\in\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})}.

This completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

Proposition 3.3.

Let Y=H2​(N)Y=H_{2}(N), where N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). Then, PSO⁡(Y)=⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ)\mathrm{PSO}(Y)=\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})}, where the generator G=−y+2(y+1)∂G=-y+2(y+1)\partial.

L−L~T∂T−1=(pT−1(y)−p~0,T(y))∂T−1+∑t=0T−2pt(y)∂t=:ST−1.\displaystyle L-\widetilde{L}_{T}\partial^{T-1}=\left(p_{T-1}(y)-\widetilde{p}_{0,T}(y)\right)\partial^{T-1}+\sum_{t=0}^{T-2}p_{t}(y)\partial^{t}=:S_{T-1}.

Note that, again, ST−1∈⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ)S_{T-1}\in\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})} if and only if ST−2∈⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ)S_{T-2}\in\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})}. By repeating this argument, we deduce that L∈⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ)L\in\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})} if and only if for some operator S1=(p1(y)−q~1(y))∂+p0(y)∈PSO(Y)S_{1}=\left(p_{1}(y)-\widetilde{q}_{1}(y)\right)\partial+p_{0}(y)\in\mathrm{PSO}(Y) we have that S1∈⟨G⟩A1​(ℝ)S_{1}\in\langle G\rangle_{A_{1}(\mathbb{R})}. L:=cy+(a1y+b1)∂+(y−3)(y+6)∂2∈PSO(Y).L:=cy+(a_{1}y+b_{1})\partial+(y-3)(y+6)\partial^{2}\in\mathrm{PSO}(Y).

But it is straightforward to see that the requirement I​E​[L​f​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[Lf(Y)\right]=0 with f⁡(y)=ynf(y)=y^{n}, and n=0,1,…,5n=0,1,\ldots,5, yields that c=0c=0, hence leading to a contradiction.

Remark 3.4.

Let N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). We conjecture that the ideal PSO​(Hp​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{p}(N)) is principle if and only if p=1,2p=1,2. Our method for proving that the ideals PSO​(H3​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{3}(N)) and PSO​(H4​(N))\text{PSO}(H_{4}(N)) are not principle could be applied to prove that the ideal PSO​(Hp​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{p}(N)) is not principle for a given p≥5p\geq 5 (assuming that this is the case), although the calculations would become increasingly complex as pp increases.

The results of Examples 3.2 and 3.3 are of interest in the context of developing the Malliavin-Stein method for distributional approximations concerning limit distributions from the third and higher order Wiener chaoses, which is a significant open problem. Since PSO​(H3​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{3}(N)) and PSO​(H4​(N))\text{PSO}(H_{4}(N)) are not principle, it means that it is less obvious a priori as to how one should determine which Stein operator(s) from the class PSO​(Hp​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{p}(N)), p≥3p\geq 3, are likely to be most well-suited for applications in the Malliavin-Stein method. Perhaps, on the flip side, there could be an added flexibility in which certain Stein operators from the class PSO​(Hp​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{p}(N)), p≥3p\geq 3, are more suited to particular applications. In any case, the appreciation that the ideal PSO​(H3​(N))\mathrm{PSO}(H_{3}(N)) is not principle is of potential value in guiding researchers in the development of the Malliavin-Stein method for limit distributions from third and higher order Wiener chaoses.

Remark 3.5.

The principle property of PSO is not invariant under addition and multiplication. This can be seen from the following simple examples. Let Y=H3​(N)Y=H_{3}(N) and X1=N3X_{1}=N^{3} and X2=−3​NX_{2}=-3N, so that Y=X1+X2Y=X_{1}+X_{2}. Then, whilst PSO​(X1)\text{PSO}(X_{1}) (this is verified by a similar argument to that given in Example 3.1; we omit the details) and PSO​(X2)\text{PSO}(X_{2}) are principle, PSO​(Y)\text{PSO}(Y) is not principle. For multiplication, we take Y=H3​(N)Y=H_{3}(N) and X3=NX_{3}=N and X4=N2−3X_{4}=N^{2}-3, so that Y=X3×X4Y=X_{3}\times X_{4}. Then, whilst PSO​(X3)\text{PSO}(X_{3}) and PSO​(X4)\text{PSO}(X_{4}) are principle, PSO​(Y)\text{PSO}(Y) is not principle.

4 Characterising feature of PSO(NN)

In this section, we study the characterising feature of PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) for N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1). It turns out to be convenient to study this problem by analysing solutions of differential equations that are satisfied by the Gaussian characteristic function. We open in Section 4.1 by developing some general theory in this direction. We also provide some simple examples of non-characterising Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution. In Section 4.2, we see that all first order polynomial Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution are characterising. We then move on to consider higher order polynomial Stein operators, for which the picture is much more complicated on account of the fact (as seen in Section 4.1) that there exist polynomial Stein operators for the standard Gaussian of order greater than one that are not characterising.

4.1 The annihilator ideal structure

Denote by φN(t)=e−t2/2\varphi_{N}(t)=e^{-t^{2}/2} the characteristic function of a standard Gaussian random variable NN. Consider the left annihilator ideal AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN):={𝒮∈A1​(ℂ):𝒮​φN=0}\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}):=\big\{\mathcal{S}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C})\,:\,\mathcal{S}\varphi_{N}=0\big\}. In virtue of Theorem 3.1 item (b), AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN)\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}) is a left principal ideal generated by the operator 𝒢=Ψ(G)=Ψ(∂−x)=∂+t\mathcal{G}=\Psi(G)=\Psi(\partial-x)=\partial+t, where Ψ\Psi is the Fourier map as introduced in Lemma 3.1, i.e.,

AnnA1​(ℂ)(φN)=⟨𝒢⟩A1​(ℂ):={𝒜𝒢:𝒜∈A1(ℂ)}.\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N})={}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}\langle\mathcal{G}\rangle:=\{\mathcal{A}\mathcal{G}\,:\,\mathcal{A}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C})\}.

In fact, following Proposition 3.1 part (d), it is generally true that, for a real-valued random variable XX, PSO​(X)\text{PSO}(X) is a principal right ideal if and only if the annihilator AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φX)\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{X}) is a left principal ideal in which the generators are linked via the Fourier map Ψ\Psi.

The annihilator ideal AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN)\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}) plays a major role in the characterising Stein operators. Obviously, every Stein operator L∈PSO​(N)L\in\text{PSO}(N) corresponds to a unique element ℒ∈AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN)\mathcal{L}\in\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}) and vice versa via the Fourier map Ψ\Psi. Let us continue with the following simple observation.

Proposition 4.1.

Let 0≠L∈PSO⁡(N)0\neq L\in\mathrm{PSO}(N) and ℒ=Ψ⁡(L)\mathcal{L}=\Psi(L) be the image of the operator LL under the Fourier map Ψ\Psi (introduced in Lemma 3.1). Then LL is a characterising Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution in the sense of Definition 1.2 if and only if

Ker(ℒ)∩𝒫^(ℝ)={e−t2/2},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathcal{L})\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})=\{e^{-t^{2}/2}\},

where 𝒫^​(ℝ)\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R}) is the class of characteristic functions of probability distributions on the real line.

Proof.

It is immediate that φN(t)=e−t2/2∈Ker(ℒ)\varphi_{N}(t)=e^{-t^{2}/2}\in\text{Ker}(\mathcal{L}) because ℒ=𝒜(t+∂)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{A}(t+\partial) for some 𝒜∈A1​(ℂ)\mathcal{A}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C}) and 𝒢φN(t)=(t+∂)e−t2/2=0\mathcal{G}\varphi_{N}(t)=(t+\partial)e^{-t^{2}/2}=0. In addition, e−t2/2≠φ∈Ker(ℒ)e^{-t^{2}/2}\neq\varphi\in\text{Ker}(\mathcal{L}) if and only if I​E​[L​f​(X)]=I​E​[L​f​(N)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Lf(X)]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Lf(N)]=0 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, where XX is a random variable whose characteristic function is φ\varphi. Hence, the claim follows. ∎

We continue with some illustrating examples. These examples show how one can construct polynomial Stein operators for the standard Gaussian of order T≥2T\geq 2 that are not characterising.

Example 4.1.

(a) Let G=x−∂∈PSO(N)G=x-\partial\in\mathrm{PSO}(N). Then, obviously, GG is a characterising Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution. This goes all the way back to Stein’s seminal paper [Ste72]. In order to apply Proposition 4.1, note that Ψ(G)=𝒢=t+∂\Psi(G)=\mathcal{G}=t+\partial and, clearly Ker(𝒢)∩𝒫^(ℝ)={e−t2/2}\text{Ker}(\mathcal{G})\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})=\{e^{-t^{2}/2}\}.

(b) Let x0∈ℝ∖{0}x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}, and consider the operator ℒ=𝒜(t+∂)∈AnnA1​(ℂ)(φN)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{A}(t+\partial)\in\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}), where 𝒜=(t−ix0)+∂∈A1(ℂ)\mathcal{A}=(t-\mathrm{i}x_{0})+\partial\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C}). One can easily check that both characteristic functions

e−t2/2,e−t2/2ei​t​x0∈Ker(ℒ)∩𝒫^(ℝ).e^{-t^{2}/2},\,e^{-t^{2}/2}e^{\mathrm{i}tx_{0}}\in\text{Ker}(\mathcal{L})\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R}).
