Hence, Proposition 4.1 entails that the operator L=Ψ−1​(ℒ)L=\Psi^{-1}(\mathcal{L}) is not a characterising Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution without assuming a further condition on the first derivative (evaluated at t=0t=0) of characteristic functions φ∈𝒫^​(ℝ)\varphi\in\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R}) (note that −i∂∂t(e−t2/2ei​t​x0)|t=0=x0≠0-\mathrm{i}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(e^{-t^{2}/2}e^{\mathrm{i}tx_{0}})\big|_{t=0}=x_{0}\neq 0). For example, with the additional assumption I​E​[X]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[X]=0 (that is φ′​(0)=0\varphi^{\prime}(0)=0), the operator LL is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) distribution.

(c) This time, let 𝒜=(t∂+2t2−1){\mathcal{A}}=(t\partial+2t^{2}-1) and ℒ=𝒜(t+∂)=(t∂2+3t2∂−∂+2t3){\mathcal{L}}={\mathcal{A}}(t+\partial)=(t\partial^{2}+3t^{2}\partial-\partial+2t^{3}). Then, one can easily check that the characteristic functions

e−t2/2,e−t2∈Ker(ℒ)∩𝒫^(ℝ)e^{-t^{2}/2},\,e^{-t^{2}}\in\text{Ker}(\mathcal{L})\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})

corresponding to the Gaussian distributions N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) and N⁡(0,2)N(0,2), respectively. Hence, operator L=Ψ−1​(ℒ)L=\Psi^{-1}(\mathcal{L}) is not a characterising Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution without assuming a further condition on the second derivative (evaluated at t=0t=0) of characteristic functions φ∈𝒫^​(ℝ)\varphi\in\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R}) (note that −∂2∂t2​(e−t2)|t=0=2-\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}(e^{-t^{2}})\big|_{t=0}=2). For example, with the additional assumption I​E​[X2]=1{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[X^{2}]=1 (that is φ′′​(0)=−1\varphi^{\prime\prime}(0)=-1), the operator LL is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) distribution.

(d) More generally, there exist TT-th order (T≥2T\geq 2) differential operators in the class PSO⁡(N)\mathrm{PSO}(N) for which T−1T-1 moment conditions must be specified for the operator SS to be characterising. Consider a mixture of Gaussian distributions YY with density pY​(x)=∑j=1Twj​pj​(x)p_{Y}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{T}w_{j}p_{j}(x), where w1,…,wT>0w_{1},\ldots,w_{T}>0, ∑j=1Twj=1\sum_{j=1}^{T}w_{j}=1 and, for j=1,…,Tj=1,\ldots,T, the function pjp_{j} is the density of a N⁡(0,σj2)N(0,\sigma_{j}^{2}) random variable, with σ12,…,σT2>0\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{T}^{2}>0 distinct and also σ12=1.\sigma_{1}^{2}=1. Since p1,…,pTp_{1},\ldots,p_{T} are linearly independent holonomic functions that satisfy first order homogeneous differential equations with polynomial coefficients, it follows that pY​(x)=∑j=1Twj​pj​(x)p_{Y}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{T}w_{j}p_{j}(x) is a holonomic function and satisfies a TT-th order homogeneous differential equation of the form L​p=0Lp=0, where L​p​(x)=∑j=0m∑k=0Taj​k​xj​p(k)​(x)Lp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\sum_{k=0}^{T}a_{jk}x^{j}p^{(k)}(x), with real-valued coefficients aj​ka_{jk} that do not depend on w1,…,wTw_{1},\ldots,w_{T} (they do not depend on w1,…,wTw_{1},\ldots,w_{T} because any linear combination of p1,…,pTp_{1},\ldots,p_{T} will satisfy L​p=0Lp=0). By a standard integration by parts argument (see, for example, the proof of Lemma 4.1 of [GMS19]) it follows that a Stein operator for YY is given by S​f​(x)=∑j=0m∑k=0T(−1)k​aj​k​∂k(xj​f​(x))Sf(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\sum_{k=0}^{T}(-1)^{k}a_{jk}\partial^{k}(x^{j}f(x)), where f∈P⁡(ℝ)f\in P(\mathbb{R}). Since the operator SS has no dependence on w1,…,wTw_{1},\ldots,w_{T}, for SS to be a characterising Stein operator for X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1), additional conditions must be specified to ensure that w1=1w_{1}=1 and w2=⋯=wT=0w_{2}=\cdots=w_{T}=0. For a characterisation based on moment conditions, T−1T-1 moments of XX would need to be specified; we do not need to specify TT moments because w1=1−∑j=2Twjw_{1}=1-\sum_{j=2}^{T}w_{j}.

The next proposition studies the structure of the annihilator ideal AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN)\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}). It turns out that the null space of the annihilator ideal AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN)\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}) is extremely large and in fact it includes any holonomic characteristic function.

Proposition 4.2.

Let

Ker(AnnA1​(ℂ)(φN)):={Ker(ℒ):ℒ∈AnnA1​(ℂ)(φN)}=⋃𝒜∈A1​(ℂ)Ker(𝒜(t+∂)).\mathrm{Ker}\big(\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N})\big):=\{\mathrm{Ker}(\mathcal{L})\,:\,\mathcal{L}\in\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N})\}=\bigcup_{\mathcal{A}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}\mathrm{Ker}\left(\mathcal{A}(t+\partial)\right).

Then

Ker⁡(AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN))∩𝒫^​(ℝ)=𝒫^​(ℝ)Hol,\mathrm{Ker}\big(\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N})\big)\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})=\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})^{\mathrm{Hol}},

where 𝒫^​(ℝ)Hol\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})^{\mathrm{Hol}} stands for the class of all holonomic characteristic functions (possibly discrete distributions, e.g. the Bernoulli distribution).

Proof.

It is clear that Ker​(AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN))∩𝒫^​(ℝ)⊆𝒫^​(ℝ)Hol\text{Ker}(\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}))\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})^{\mathrm{Hol}}. For the other inclusion, let φ∈𝒫^​(ℝ)Hol\varphi\in\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})^{\mathrm{Hol}}. Then, there is ℒ∈A1​(ℂ)\mathcal{L}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C}) such that ℒ​φ=0\mathcal{L}\varphi=0. On the other hand, by the left Ore property, one can write 𝒮ℒ=𝒜(t+∂)\mathcal{S}\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{A}(t+\partial) for some elements 𝒮,𝒜∈A1​(ℂ)\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A}\in A_{1}(\mathbb{C}). Hence, 𝒜(t+∂)∈AnnA1​(ℂ)(φN)\mathcal{A}(t+\partial)\in\text{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}) and 𝒜(t+∂)φ=0\mathcal{A}(t+\partial)\varphi=0. Therefore, φ∈Ker(𝒜(t+∂))\varphi\in\text{Ker}(\mathcal{A}(t+\partial)) and we are done. ∎

4.2 Characterising Stein operators for the Gaussian distribution

In the following proposition, we show that first order polynomial Stein equations for the Gaussian distribution are characterising in the sense of Definition 1.2. An immediate consequence is that Stein operator Sm:=Hm−1∂−Hm∈PSO(N)S_{m}:=H_{m-1}\partial-H_{m}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N), m≥1m\geq 1, of [GR05] is characterising.

Proposition 4.3.

Let q∈ℝ⁡[x]q\in\mathbb{R}[x] be a non-zero polynomial with real coefficients and δ\delta stands for the adjoint operator. Then, the operator

L=q(x)∂−δq(x)∈PSO(N)L=q(x)\partial-\delta q(x)\in\mathrm{PSO}(N)

is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution in the sense of Definition 1.2.

In particular, the operator Sm:=Hm−1∂−Hm∈PSO(N)S_{m}:=H_{m-1}\partial-H_{m}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N), m≥1m\geq 1, is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution.

Proof.

We first note the following simple connection between the Stein operator q(x)∂−δq(x)q(x)\partial-\delta q(x) and the classical Stein operator ∂−x\partial-x. Consider the Stein operator f′​(x)−x​f​(x)f^{\prime}(x)-xf(x). Let f⁡(x)=q⁡(x)​g​(x)f(x)=q(x)g(x). Then f′​(x)−x​f​(x)=q⁡(x)​g′​(x)−δ​q​(x)​g​(x)f^{\prime}(x)-xf(x)=q(x)g^{\prime}(x)-\delta q(x)g(x). Now, let XX be a real-valued random variable with density pX​(x)p_{X}(x) and suppose that I​E​[q⁡(X)​g′​(X)−δ​q​(X)​g​(X)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[q(X)g^{\prime}(X)-\delta q(X)g(X)]=0 for all g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} for some suitable class of functions 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Then, by an integration by parts argument, we have that ∫ℝ(pX′​(x)+x​pX​(x))​q​(x)​g​(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{\mathbb{R}}(p_{X}^{\prime}(x)+xp_{X}(x))q(x)g(x)\,dx=0 for all g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}. We thus deduce that pX​(x)p_{X}(x) satisfies the ODE pX′​(x)+x​pX​(x)=0p_{X}^{\prime}(x)+xp_{X}(x)=0. On solving this ODE subject to the condition that pX​(x)p_{X}(x) is the probability density function of a real-valued random variable (so that OPEN∫ℝpX​(x)​𝑑x=1)\int_{\mathbb{R}}p_{X}(x)\,dx=1) we deduce that pX(x)=(2π)−1/2e−x2/2p_{X}(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2}, and therefore X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1).

That the operator Sm:=Hm−1∂−Hm∈PSO(N)S_{m}:=H_{m-1}\partial-H_{m}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution now follows on taking q​(x)=Hm−1​(x)q(x)=H_{m-1}(x) and using that δ​Hm−1​(x)=Hm​(x)\delta H_{m-1}(x)=H_{m}(x) (see Definition 2.10). ∎

We now consider the characterising property of higher order Stein operators. In the light of part (d) of Example 4.1, we know that there exist many higher order Stein operators that are not characterising. Our aim here is to attempt to give some examples of general classes of higher order polynomial Stein operators for the Gaussian distribution that are characterising. The most natural operator to start with is perhaps the higher order counterpart of the Stein operator SmS_{m} given in Proposition 4.3, namely the Stein operator Lm=∂m−Hm(x)L_{m}=\partial^{m}-H_{m}(x), m≥1m\geq 1. As noted in the introduction, the fact that Lm∈PSO⁡(N)L_{m}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N), m≥1m\geq 1, was known to [GR05]. The proof of the following proposition is technical and is given in Appendix A.

Proposition 4.4.

Let m≥1m\geq 1 be fixed. Then, the operator Lm=∂m−Hm∈PSO(N)L_{m}=\partial^{m}-H_{m}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution among those random variables that are symmetric (that is X=d−XX=_{d}-X) and have an infinitely divisible distribution. When m=1,2,3m=1,2,3, the characterisation holds without the need for the symmetric and infinitely divisible distribution assumptions.

Remark 4.1.

In Proposition 4.4, our characterisation of the standard Gaussian distribution has additional symmetry and infinite divisibility conditions when m≥4m\geq 4. We conjecture that these additional conditions are not necessary to ensure characterisation, but are rather artefacts resulting from our proof. We leave it as an interesting open problem to verify or disprove this conjecture. Similar comments apply for Corollary 4.1 and Proposition 4.5 below.

We can generalise Proposition 4.4 to deduce a characterisation result for the Stein operators S(k,t)=Hk∂t−Hk+t∈PSO(N)S(k,t)=H_{k}\partial^{t}-H_{k+t}\in\text{PSO}(N), k,t≥1k,t\geq 1. Recall that the fact that S⁡(k,t)∈PSO⁡(N)S(k,t)\in\mathrm{PSO}(N), k,t≥1k,t\geq 1, was known to [Bar86].

Corollary 4.1.

Let k,t≥1k,t\geq 1. Then, the operator Hk∂t−Hk+t∈PSO(N)H_{k}\partial^{t}-H_{k+t}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a characterising Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distributions among those random variables that are symmetric and have an infinitely divisible distribution. When t=1,2,3t=1,2,3, the characterisation holds without the need for the symmetric and infinitely divisible distribution assumptions.

Proof.

We deduce the result from Proposition 4.4 by applying the technique used in the proof of Proposition 4.3. Consider the Stein operator ∂tf⁡(x)−Ht​(x)​f​(x)\partial^{t}f(x)-H_{t}(x)f(x). Now, let XX be a real-valued random variable with density pX​(x)p_{X}(x) and suppose that I​E​[f(t)​(X)−Ht​(X)​f​(X)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[f^{(t)}(X)-H_{t}(X)f(X)]=0 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} for some suitable class of functions ℱ\mathcal{F}. Then, by an integration by parts argument, we have that ∫ℝf⁡(x)​T​pX​(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)Tp_{X}(x)\,dx=0 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, for some linear differential operator TT (the particular form that the operator TT takes is not important to our argument). We thus deduce that pX​(x)p_{X}(x) satisfies the ODE T​pX​(x)=0Tp_{X}(x)=0. By proposition 4.4, we can infer that the only solution to this ODE that satisfies the properties of a probability density function is pX(x)=(2π)−1/2e−x2/2p_{X}(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2} if t=1,2,3t=1,2,3, and again pX(x)=(2π)−1/2e−x2/2p_{X}(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2} if we impose the additional assumptions that pX​(x)p_{X}(x) must be the density of a symmetric and infinitely divisible random variable when t≥4t\geq 4.

Now, let f⁡(x)=Hk​(x)​g​(x)f(x)=H_{k}(x)g(x). Then we get that ∂tf⁡(x)−Ht​(x)​f​(x)=Hk​(x)​∂tg⁡(x)−Hk+t​(x)​g​(x)\partial^{t}f(x)-H_{t}(x)f(x)=H_{k}(x)\partial^{t}g(x)-H_{k+t}(x)g(x). Let YY be a real-valued random variable with density pY​(x)p_{Y}(x) and suppose that I​E​[Hk​(Y)​g(t)​(Y)−Hk+t​(Y)​g​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[H_{k}(Y)g^{(t)}(Y)-H_{k+t}(Y)g(Y)]=0 for all g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} for some suitable class of functions 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Then, by the same integration by parts argument as before, we have that ∫ℝHk​(x)​g​(x)​T​pY​(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{\mathbb{R}}H_{k}(x)g(x)Tp_{Y}(x)\,dx=0 for all g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}, where TT is the same operator as introduced earlier in this proof. We thus deduce that pY​(x)p_{Y}(x) satisfies the ODE T​pY​(x)=0Tp_{Y}(x)=0, the same ODE as satisfied by pX​(x)p_{X}(x). Thus, under the relevant assumptions for the cases t=1,2,3t=1,2,3 and t≥4t\geq 4, the only solution that satisfies the properties of a probability density function is pY(x)=(2π)−1/2e−x2/2p_{Y}(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2}, and therefore Y∼N⁡(0,1)Y\sim N(0,1). ∎

Another interesting class of higher order Stein operators for the standard Gaussian distribution can be derived via the so-called Rodriguez formula for Hermite polynomials. In fact, the Rodriguez formula implies that the characteristic function φN(t)=e−t2/2\varphi_{N}(t)=e^{-t^{2}/2} satisfies the ODE

∂mφN​(t)=(−1)m​Hm​(t)​φN​(t),∀m≥1.\partial^{m}\varphi_{N}(t)=(-1)^{m}H_{m}(t)\varphi_{N}(t),\quad\forall\,m\geq 1. (4.1)

Let ℛm=∂m−(−1)mHm∈AnnA1​(ℂ)(φN)\mathcal{R}_{m}=\partial^{m}-(-1)^{m}H_{m}\in\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}) and hence Rm=Ψ−1(ℛm)=(−1)mHm(−i∂)−imxm∈PSO(N)R_{m}=\Psi^{-1}(\mathcal{R}_{m})=(-1)^{m}H_{m}(-\mathrm{i}\partial)-\mathrm{i}^{m}x^{m}\in\text{PSO}(N) (possibly after a multiplication by a suitable power of i\mathrm{i} to get real coefficients). The polynomial Stein operators RmR_{m} are particularly interesting whenever the sole mm-th moment matching I​E​[Xm]=I​E​[Nm]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[X^{m}]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[N^{m}] is applicable. The proof of the following proposition is given in Appendix A.

Proposition 4.5.

Let m≥1m\geq 1 be fixed. Then, the operator Rm=(−1)mHm(−i∂)−imxm∈PSO(N)R_{m}=(-1)^{m}H_{m}(-\mathrm{i}\partial)-\mathrm{i}^{m}x^{m}\in\mathrm{PSO}(N) is a characterising polynomial Stein operator for the standard Gaussian distribution among those random variables that are symmetric and have an infinitely divisible distribution. When m=1,2,3m=1,2,3, the characterisation holds without the need for the symmetric and infinitely divisible distribution assumptions.

5 A general result on the characterising feature of polynomial Stein operators

In Section 4, we saw examples of non-trivial elements of PSO​(N)\text{PSO}(N) that are not characterising in the sense of Definition 1.2. This non-characterising property in fact applies for any distribution with a holonomic density or holonomic characteristic function, and is a consequence of the following general theorem.

Theorem 5.1.

Fix n≥1n\geq 1. Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be continuous random variables. Suppose that the characteristic functions of X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} are holonomic, or X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} have holonomic densities. Then

PSO⁡(X1)∩⋯∩PSO⁡(Xn)≠{0}.\mathrm{PSO}(X_{1})\cap\cdots\cap\mathrm{PSO}(X_{n})\neq\{0\}. (5.1)
Proof.

First note that the assumption that the characteristic functions of X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} are holonomic implies that PSO​(Xk)≠{0}\text{PSO}(X_{k})\neq\{0\} for each k=1,…,nk=1,\ldots,n, by Proposition 3.1, item (a). Similarly, the assumption that densities of X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} are holonomic implies that PSO​(Xk)≠{0}\text{PSO}(X_{k})\neq\{0\} for each k=1,…,nk=1,\ldots,n, by Proposition 3.1, item (b). On the other hand, by Stafford’s Theorem 2.2 each right ideal PSO​(Xk)=⟨G1k,G2k⟩\text{PSO}(X_{k})=\langle G^{k}_{1},G^{k}_{2}\rangle for two generators G1kG^{k}_{1} and G2kG^{k}_{2}. Since Weyl algebras are right Noetherian integral domains they are right Ore domains [MR87, Theorem 1.15]. Therefore, letting R=A1​(ℝ)R=A_{1}(\mathbb{R}), we have

⋂k=1nG1k​R∩G2k​R≠{0}.\bigcap_{k=1}^{n}G^{k}_{1}R\cap G^{k}_{2}R\neq\{0\}.

On the other hand, G1k​R∩G2k​R⊆PSO​(Xk)G^{k}_{1}R\cap G^{k}_{2}R\subseteq\text{PSO}(X_{k}) for each k=1,…,nk=1,\ldots,n, and whence the claim follows. ∎

Corollary 5.1.

Let N∼N⁡(0,1)N\sim N(0,1) and XX be a continuous random variable whose characteristic function is holonomic, or whose density is holonomic. Then

PSO⁡(N)∩PSO⁡(X)≠{0}.\mathrm{PSO}(N)\cap\mathrm{PSO}(X)\neq\{0\}.
Remark 5.1.

(a) In the statement of Theorem 5.1, the supports of the random variables X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} do not need to be the same. In fact, one can even consider random variables having disjoint supports. Let XX and YY be two continuous random variables whose characteristic functions are holonomic or whose densities are holonomic with disjoint supports 𝔻X\mathbb{D}_{X} and 𝔻Y\mathbb{D}_{Y}, respectively. Let 𝕌X\mathbb{U}_{X} and 𝕌Y\mathbb{U}_{Y} be two disjoint open domains so that 𝕌X⊇𝔻X\mathbb{U}_{X}\supseteq\mathbb{D}_{X}, 𝕌Y⊇𝔻Y\mathbb{U}_{Y}\supseteq\mathbb{D}_{Y}. It is evident that I​E​[SX​f​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[S_{X}f(Y)]=0 for all f∈𝒮⁡(𝕌X)f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{U}_{X}), where SX∈PSO​(X)S_{X}\in\text{PSO}(X). In addition, clearly 𝒮⁡(𝕌X)⊆𝒮⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{U}_{X})\subseteq\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}); however, the requirement I​E​[SX​f​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[S_{X}f(Y)]=0 for all f∈𝒮⁡(ℝ)f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) is a non-trivial task. According to Theorem 5.1 there is at least one non-trivial polynomial differential operator S≠0S\neq 0 such that

IE[Sf(Xk)]=0,∀f∈𝒮(ℝ)⊇𝒮(𝕌),k=1,…,n,{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Sf(X_{k})]=0,\quad\forall\,f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})\supseteq\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{U}),\quad k=1,\ldots,n,

where each 𝔻Xk\mathbb{D}_{X_{k}} is the support of random variable XkX_{k}, and the open domain 𝕌⊇𝔻X1∪⋯∪𝔻Xn\mathbb{U}\supseteq\mathbb{D}_{X_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup\mathbb{D}_{X_{n}}. An example of an operator 0≠L∈PSO​(N)∩PSO​(X)0\neq L\in\text{PSO}(N)\cap\text{PSO}(X) is given in [AGG23b, Section 3.1] when XX is distributed as a semi-circular distribution with probability density function pX​(x)=(2/π)​1−x2​1[−1,1]p_{X}(x)=(2/\pi)\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\textbf{1}_{[-1,1]} supported on the interval [−1,1][-1,1].

(b) Theorem 5.1 is also related to characterising Stein operators; see Definition 1.2. Firstly, in order that a polynomial Stein operator would be useful from a probabilistic point of view, the class ℱ\mathcal{F} of test functions must contain functions being non-zero on the support of the underlying target random variable. Secondly, for random variables XX and YY as in part (a) of this remark, Theorem 5.1 yields the existence of a polynomial Stein operator S≠0S\not=0 so that I​E​[S​f​(X)]=I​E​[S​f​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Sf(X)]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Sf(Y)]=0 for all f∈𝒮⁡(ℝ)f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}). Therefore, the Stein operator SS cannot be a characterising operator for neither XX nor YY without any extra assumption; see also Example 4.1.

Appendix A Further proofs

Proof of Proposition 4.4. The case m=1m=1 corresponds to the classical standard Gaussian Stein operator ∂−x\partial-x, so we focus on the case m≥2m\geq 2. Recall that Lm=∂m−Hm(x)L_{m}=\partial^{m}-H_{m}(x). Then applying the mapping ℒm=Ψ⁡(Lm)\mathcal{L}_{m}=\Psi(L_{m}) we have that ℒm=imtm−Hm(−i∂)\mathcal{L}_{m}=\mathrm{i}^{m}t^{m}-H_{m}(-\mathrm{i}\partial), and ℒm∈AnnA1​(ℂ)​(φN)\mathcal{L}_{m}\in\mathrm{Ann}_{A_{1}(\mathbb{C})}(\varphi_{N}). We shall employ the technique for proving sufficiency of Stein characterisations from our recent paper [AGG23b] to prove that Ker(ℒm)∩𝒫^(ℝ)={e−t2/2}\mathrm{Ker}(\mathcal{L}_{m})\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})=\{e^{-t^{2}/2}\} for m=2,3m=2,3 under no additional assumptions on the random variable XX, and for m≥4m\geq 4 under the assumption that the random variable XX is symmetric and has an infinitely divisible distribution.

Consider the ODE

ℒm​φ​(t)=0.\mathcal{L}_{m}\varphi(t)=0. (A.1)

This ODE has an essential singularity at t=∞t=\infty, and so we seek asymptotic approximations for the solutions using the ansatz φ⁡(t)=eS⁡(1/t)\varphi(t)=e^{S(1/t)}. Using this ansatz and the method of dominate balance (see [BO99, Chapter 3] for a detailed account of this method) we deduce that OPENS′​(1/t))m∼t3​mS^{\prime}(1/t))^{m}\sim t^{3m}, as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. We thus deduce that there are mm linearly independent solutions to the ODE (A.1) with the following asymptotic behaviour as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty,

φj,m(t)=exp(−ωmj−1​t22(1+o(1))),j=1,…,m,\varphi_{j,m}(t)=\exp\bigg(-\frac{\omega_{m}^{j-1}t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg),\quad j=1,\ldots,m,

where ωm\omega_{m} is the mm-th root of unity (recall that 1,ωm,…,ωmm−11,\omega_{m},\ldots,\omega_{m}^{m-1} are the mm distinct roots of the polynomial xm−1x^{m}-1). The general solution of the ODE (A.1) is given by

φ⁡(t)=∑j=1mCj,m​φj,m​(t)\varphi(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}C_{j,m}\varphi_{j,m}(t) (A.2)

for some arbitrary constants C1,m,…,Cm,mC_{1,m},\ldots,C_{m,m}. Note that φ1,m​(t)=exp⁡(−(t2/2)​(1+o⁡(1)))\varphi_{1,m}(t)=\exp(-(t^{2}/2)(1+o(1))), as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty; this asymptotic behaviour is consistent with that of the characteristic function e−t2/2e^{-t^{2}/2} of the standard Gaussian distribution. If we can argue that φm​(t)\varphi_{m}(t) can only be a characteristic function if C2,m=⋯=Cm,m=0C_{2,m}=\cdots=C_{m,m}=0, then it follows that Ker(ℒm)∩𝒫^(ℝ)={e−t2/2}\mathrm{Ker}(\mathcal{L}_{m})\cap\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbb{R})=\{e^{-t^{2}/2}\}, meaning that LmL_{m} is a characterising Stein operator.

We first consider the case m=2m=2. In this case, φ2,2​(t)=exp⁡((t2/2)​(1+o⁡(1)))\varphi_{2,2}(t)=\exp((t^{2}/2)(1+o(1))), as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, and so this solution is unbounded as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. Since characteristic functions are bounded, in order for φ2​(t)\varphi_{2}(t) to be a characteristic function we must take C2,2=0C_{2,2}=0, and so L2L_{2} is a characterising Stein operator. Similarly, the solutions φ2,3​(t)\varphi_{2,3}(t) and φ3,3​(t)\varphi_{3,3}(t) blow up as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, and so we deduce by the same argument that L3L_{3} is a characterising Stein operator.

Suppose now that m≥4m\geq 4. It is no longer the case that all solutions except for φ1,m​(t)\varphi_{1,m}(t) are unbounded as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, and so the argument used to treat the cases m=2,3m=2,3 is no longer enough to deduce that the operator LmL_{m} is characterising. To deal with this difficulty, we introduce the additional assumptions that the distribution of XX is symmetric and infinitely divisible. We shall exploit the properties that the characteristic function φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) of an infinitely divisible distribution is non-zero for all tt, and that the characteristic function of a symmetric random variable is real-valued.

Suppose m≥4m\geq 4 is even; the odd mm case is similar, and so is omitted. Let Rj,mR_{j,m} and Ij,mI_{j,m} denote the real and imaginary parts of ωj−1\omega^{j-1} for j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m. Then applying Euler’s formula ei​x=cos⁡(x)+i​sin⁡(x)e^{\mathrm{i}x}=\cos(x)+\mathrm{i}\sin(x) to the solution (A.2) gives the following alternative representation of the general solution:

φm​(t)=∑j=1maj,m​gj,m​(t),\varphi_{m}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j,m}g_{j,m}(t),

where a1,m,…,am,ma_{1,m},\ldots,a_{m,m} are arbitrary constants, and, as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty,

g1,m​(t)\displaystyle g_{1,m}(t) =exp⁡(−t22​(1+o⁡(1))),gm/2,m​(t)=exp⁡(t22​(1+o⁡(1))),\displaystyle=\exp\bigg(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg),\quad g_{m/2,m}(t)=\exp\bigg(\frac{t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg),
gj,m​(t)\displaystyle g_{j,m}(t) =sin(Ij,m​t22(1+o(1)))exp(−Rj,m​t22(1+o(1))),j=2,…,m/2−1,\displaystyle=\sin\bigg(\frac{I_{j,m}t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg)\exp\bigg(-\frac{R_{j,m}t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg),\quad j=2,\ldots,m/2-1,
gj,m​(t)\displaystyle g_{j,m}(t) =cos(Ij,m​t22(1+o(1)))exp(−Rj,m​t22(1+o(1))),j=m/2+1,…,m.\displaystyle=\cos\bigg(\frac{I_{j,m}t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg)\exp\bigg(-\frac{R_{j,m}t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg),\quad j=m/2+1,\ldots,m.

Now, gm/2​(t)→∞g_{m/2}(t)\rightarrow\infty as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, so we must take am/2,m=0a_{m/2,m}=0. We note that Ij,m≠0I_{j,m}\not=0 and Rj,m<1R_{j,m}<1 for j∈{2,…,m/2−1}∪{m/2+1,…,m}j\in\{2,\ldots,m/2-1\}\cup\{m/2+1,\ldots,m\}. Moreover, the symmetric distribution assumption ensures that the solution φm​(t)\varphi_{m}(t) is real-valued. Due to the infinitely divisible distribution assumption, φm​(t)\varphi_{m}(t) cannot equal to zero for any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, and we are now forced to take a2,m=⋯=am,m=0a_{2,m}=\cdots=a_{m,m}=0, which implies that the Stein operator LmL_{m} is characterising. □\Box

Proof of Proposition 4.5. Following the same steps as in the proof of Proposition 4.4 yields that the general solution to the ODE ℛm​φm​(t)=0\mathcal{R}_{m}\varphi_{m}(t)=0 is given by φm​(t)=∑j=1mBj,m​φ~j,m​(t)\varphi_{m}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}B_{j,m}\tilde{\varphi}_{j,m}(t) for some arbitrary constants B1,m,…,Bm,mB_{1,m},\ldots,B_{m,m}, and, as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty,

φ~j,m(t)=exp(−ωmj−1​t22(1+o(1))),j=1,…,m.\tilde{\varphi}_{j,m}(t)=\exp\bigg(-\frac{\omega_{m}^{j-1}t^{2}}{2}(1+o(1))\bigg),\quad j=1,\ldots,m.

To leading order, the linearly independent solutions φ~j,m​(t)\tilde{\varphi}_{j,m}(t), j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m, have precisely the same asymptotic behaviour as the linearly independent solutions φj,m​(t)\varphi_{j,m}(t), j=1,…,mj=1,\ldots,m, from the proof of Proposition 4.4. Reasoning exactly as we did in the proof of Proposition 4.4 now completes the proof. □\Box
